speechtext:
The situation in China,
as I understand it, is in the nature of a civil war, and the action to which my hon. friend refers is not so much, from the point of view of Japan, active external aggression as it is action taken to defend some of its nationals in a particular area. China and Japan are both members of the League of Nations, and if China felt that she was being attacked aggressively I assume that she would have made some representations to the League of Nations. The provisions of the league require that when any request of the kind is submitted all countries which are parties to the league shall be so informed. Canada has received no information from the secretary general of the league that any representations have been made by China that she is 'being attacked, and certainly this government has not felt that Canada has any special responsibility to take action while all other nations refrain from so doing, or await representations by China on her own behalf.

speechtext:
In my judgment there is a weakness in the wording of this amendment, as far as the returned soldier is concerned; apparently it holds out to the returned soldier a preference because of his service overseas, but it is not so worded as to give him that preference beyond any doubt. I refer particularly to the words, "other qualifications being equal." It would be very easy to tell a returned soldier, "Yes, you have the qualifications necessary to fill this position, but your qualifications are not so great as
the qualifications of another man." It does seem to me, if you want really to give the soldier the preference to which he is entitled, you should specify that he possesses the qualifications necessary to fill the position. For example, you might have a returned soldier who was thoroughly qualified to fill the position. He might be put in competition with a man applying for the same position, and who was a graduate of a university. From an educational standpoint, I suppose the second man would be superior to the first, and yet the returned soldier might possess all the qualifications required satisfactorily and effectively to perform the duties of that office. It leaves it open to the minister or to the board to get out of giving the returned soldier the preference to which he is entitled.

Since no devout supporter of the government has
National Revenue Act

enough gratitude in his heart to congratulate the opposition, I think it belongs properly to one who is not affiliated with either party, to outline once more the curious influence which Toryism exercises upon certain departments, and upon certain members of the government.
The question of whether the returned soldier should be given preference or not is a very wide one. I think we have gone far enough in that direction. I am second to none in rendering honour to Canadians who served in the army, but, at the same time, there are many good Canadians who served their country by working in Canada and for Canada. We are undermining to a large degree the sense of patriotism and citizenship by always bringing to the front the soldiers, whether they belonged to the Canadian army or to the British army, as people who deserve gratitude and preference over the Canadian citizen who has worked all his life in perhaps a simpler capacity, but certainly in as useful a capacity, as far as Canada is concerned, as by serving in the army.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: A safer capacity.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Safer for Canada, yes.
I fail to see where many of the most outspoken and especially noisy upholders of everything militaristic have, either in the last war or in preceding wars, given evidence of their desire to serve in a non-safe capacity. I have noticed very frequently that the real soldier, the man who went to the fields and fought battles, is usually more modest than the politician who makes such a noise about it. That is one point.
The other point is the one raised by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power). Are we going to allow the habits of the administration to grow to the extent where no difference is to be made, in preferment, or otherwise, as between the men who acknowledge themselves servants of Canada primarily -whether they believe in the co-operation of Canada in British wars or not, whether they take the point of view of Canadianism or that of British imperialism and Imperial cooperation, is an entirely different question- and the British soldiers?
Consider what the government of Great Britain does for its own people, and what the government of Australia does. I do not think you will find in any statute of Great Britain or of Australia any disposition to put on the same footing as their own people Canadians who may have served accidentally in the army of Great Britain or the Australian militia. You would not find it in India; you would not find it in South Africa, and you would not find it in any British statute. Quite properly, the British look to their own 
people first; Australia looks to its people first, and South Africa does the same. I think the Canadian government and the Canadian parliament should look to their people first also.
Therefore, the proposal made by the hon. member for Quebec South should recommend itself to the attention of the house, and I think to the attention especially of the members sitting to the right of the Speaker. Perhaps the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Euler) may be able to take some little inspiration from his friends, rather than to give way so complacently to the opponents of his government and of his party.

That the said bill be not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole with instructions that they have power to amend the same by providing that (a) customs appraisers of all classes whether serving at the various ports and places of entry or as dominion appraisers; (b) All officers in the customs-excise preventive service; and (c) All officers assigned to duty as investigators of values and claims for drawback, shall be appointed by the Civil Service Commission after public competition and examination by the Civil Service Commission in association with such representatives of the department as may be named by the minister and any others that he may think necessary to properly determine their qualifications.
I do not propose to trespass upon the time of the house further than to say that it is essential that we should maintain in its integrity the principle of appointments to office being made by the Civil Service Commission. I yesterday directed attention to t)he observations made by the hon. Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Euler) when as a member of a select committee in 1921 he pointed out that technical and professional positions dhould only be filled after consultation between the Civil Service Commission and the deputy head or head of the department that might be affected.
The amendment which we now propose is one that in practice has been found to work out satisfactorily. Upon inquiry I find that only within the last three weeks or less it has been necessary to appoint appraisers, and that an examination was conducted by the Civil Service Commission, with the aid of officials named by the department, together with two business men in Toronto, who assisted in determining the qualifications of the various applicants.
What we ask is that in a matter of this kind, where very important interests are involved, there should be afforded the opportunity by public competition to select those persons who, by reason of the examination they have passed, and the demeanor they have shown before the minister or the deputy or the persons named by him and such other persons as may be selected for the purpose by the minister, have demonstrated their fitness to discharge the duties of the position. Appraisers, drawback investigators, and those in the preventive service, will thus be selected from a body of men whose political faith need not and will not be considered at all. The
[The Chairman.]
bill as it now stands provides that the recommendations shall be made in a certain way, and that really the minister himself shall determine who shall be appointed, and the Civil Service Commission is merely mentioned for the purpose, as I said yesterday, of permitting some use to be made of its name without in fact any value being attached to what it may do. Under these circumstances, without trespassing further on the time of the house in view of the engagements of the minister, I merely content myself with moving the amendment, and protesting against removing from the jurisdiction of the Civil Service Commission the appointment of these appraisers and drawback investigators, who will deal with very important matters in which political consideration may prevail, as well as in the performance of their duties by members of the preventive service, which is so very important.

I am going to establish an examining body within the Department of National Revenue, and ask them from time to time to examine and make selections from those who may apply for these positions. That will be a body in which I have confidence, and naturally I shall feel that the persons they select will be of value to me. But before adding - them to the personnel, I shall refer their names to the Civil Service Commission for a decision from that incompetent body from which I am taking away the whole administration of this work. He is in effect saying: I have a board within my department in which I have confidence, and which is competent to select the proper applicants, but in order to delude the public, in order to blind their eyes to the real facts of the matter, I am going to refer their names to the Civil Service Commission with the proviso that if
within fifteen days they do not approve of the nominations by the departmental advisory board, the governor in council shall decide. Well, Mr. Speaker, I have my own opinion about the decisions of the governor in council. In effect, this is patronage at its very worst. The situation then, briefly, is this. The minister is going to place these particular positions which are mentioned in this bill definitely under the administration of wide-open patronage.
I think it would be as well for the minister before voting finally on the bill-although I have no hope of changing his course-to turn his attention for a moment or two to the situation in the United States. It is not all that it might be, but it is a good deal better than it was some time ago. We all know of course that whatever government is in power seeks to restrict the operation of appointments under the merit system. All governments, irrespective of party, desire more definitely the restoration of the patronage system, but particularly is this the case with the present government. In fact its predecessors introduced the merit principle. In the United States I find that exactly the same excuses were used for the continuation of patronage in making appointments to the civil service that the minister is now using for wide-open patronage in his department. When the Volstead Act was passed by congress appointments to the prohibition enforcement bureau were exempted from the provisions of the civil service law, on the plea that it would be necessary for the executive to be free to get men of character to enforce the law. I need not call the attention of the house to the results. They were certainly notorious and hopeless, and were best descirbed in the organ, known as Good Government, published by the Civil Service Reform League of the United States, in these terms:
Everyone knows that a large proportion of that force is composed of grafters, thugs and miscreants, who not only take bribes, but are guilty 'of unlawful acts of violence.
And further:
In the beginning the league pointed out the probability of this result if the positions were exempted from the provisions of the civil service law, and has endeavored constantly to procure an amendment of the law which would classify the entire prohibition force without covering in the present members. . .
Certainly a force appointed after competitive civil service examination, and investigation of the character of the applicants by an independent body such as the Civil Service Commission, would eliminate a large proportion of such scalawags as are now appointed on political recommendations, and would vastly improve the character of the service.
The Winnipeg Tribune1, commenting upon that article, states:
National Revenue Act

Abandonment of the merit system and resort to patronage in precisely that arm of the service which is most exposed to temptation, and resort to patronage where the work demands the most absolute integrity, is inexcusable. It is amazing to find responsible cabinet ministers so blinded by partisan prejudice and so selfcomplacent.
Very strong words. They are words that I would accept and voice as my own. It is not necessary, of course, to convince students of political science that the patronage system is not the system by which you will get men of high moral character and the best qualified for responsible positions. Contemporary history shows us that. As an illustration- I think it was used by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) yesterday- I was interested in finding out just how many of those persons who were recommended for dismissal by the customs commission had been appointed under the old patronage system or by -the Civil Service Commission. I wrote to the commission under date of April 17 last, and I have their reply in my hand, signed by the secretary, Mr. Foran:

In reply to your letter of the 16th instant, I beg to say that of the customs employees who *were recommended for dismissal or retirement by the customs committee, not one was an appointee of the Civil Service Commission. W. Foran,
Secretary.
Not one was an appointee of the Civil Service Commission. I am not going to be so discourteous to my hon. friend as to suggest for one moment that the appointments he is likely to approve of will be of the scalawag or the notoriously immoral or bad type; but I say definitely to him now that he is opening the way to the widest kind of patronage,, which in the very course of human nature will lead to just that condition of affairs at some time or other-possibly not during his control of the department. I hope not, at least, for I have a good deal of confidence in him. But he is weakening not only the position of the government with respect to the Civil Service Commission, but their declarations of their belief in the merit system.

There are members of this house who believe that and they have a perfect right to that belief. Slow but sure is the motto, or one word at a time, and the launching of the plan has been entrusted to the Hon. Mr. Euler, Minister of National Revenue. The word he has chosen for the initiation of his prodigious effort is the word "merit."

Looking on this bill, as I do, as being a retrograde step on the part of the government, after the operation for some years of the Civil Service Commission, I may be pardoned if I wish to take a few minutes in recording my views on this question. I would ask also that the views of the customs officials of my own province, and other western provinces, be recorded.
The Minister of Railways just asked what was the principle of the United Farmers of Alberta regarding this question. I think that he of all men should know that the large organized farmer bodies in western Canada have for years advocated the adoption of the merit system. He has been a member of these bodies, and the Canadian Council of Agriculture has for many years maintained as one of the planks in their platform abolition of political patronage.
National Revenue Act

I cannot help but remark that there has been a tendency for some years to discredit the work of the Civil Service Commission, and the cabinet now seems disposed to make all the appointments possible, and to ignore the Civil Service Act. It is surely admitted that since confederation the need has been felt for one central co-ordinating body, to take cognizance of the various departments of the public service, to harmonize and to give system and unity to the whole administrative organization.
In looking up this question during the past few days I find that Sir George Murray, in his report of 1912, emphatically declared that duplication and topheaviness in the various departments was due to the want of some co-ordinating authority empowered to deal with the staff and organization of the departs ment, so as to secure the utmost eoonomy and efficiency in the public service. I feel that the present dissatisfaction-indeed, I was going to say chaos, and perhaps that word is not too strong-is due to the want of a body whose authority and jurisdiction would cover the whole service. I think it is wrong at the present time to undermine the work of the Civil Service Commission by an act of this kind.
In the report of the commission in 1918 regarding the printing bureau, I find they said that under any but governmental ownership the sheriff would long ago have closed the door. In the report of the parliamentary committee of 1923, the question of the co-ordination of the activities of the government was dealt with at considerable length, and several precedents were quoted. In this connection the following recommendation was made:
Another proposal which merits exploration, is an appropriate adaptation of the so-called "Business manager plan" which has evoked universal commendation in its application to municipal government.
It is to be feared that during the life of the last parliament some of the evils were accentuated by the fact that too many appointments were made notwithstanding the Civil Service Act. I cannot look upon the present bill but as a part of a plan for the continuation of that practice.
A man who has been in the civil service in Ottawa for a good many years came into my office a little while ago and said that he was tired of the whole thing. He stated that in the room in which he worked there were as many as eleven employees and he assured me that seven or less would be sufficient to do every bit of the work that was needed to be done in that roorp. He was an honest boy
[Mr. Evans.l
and the impression he left was that he was never allowed to do his best and that he was tired day after day of having to kill time.
Instead of the government taking upon itself the appointment of civil servants to administer certain branches in the several departments, it should without delay so augment the commission, if need be, that some co-ordinating method might be adopted in the service either by a kind of general manager or some central authority who could oversee the work of all the departments and branches without the terrible waste and overmanning which now exist and which in themselves are not only very expensive for the country but degrading to the employees themselves, as the effect must be detrimental to the character of everyone. As I said the other day, it has surprised me that a bill of this kind has come forward, especially seeing the views of the ministers so well recorded in Hansard some years ago. I first of all look at the words of the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), who expressed himself on March 11, 19211, as follows:
Mr. Speaker, I endorse the remarks of the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) and I am opposed to the resolution moved by the hon. member for Victoria. I do not believe in political patronage. It has been tried in many countries of the world, and it has been found wanting everywhere. I think that positions should go to merit and never to influence, on the part either of the candidates themselves or of their families, and I am opposed to nepotism in the distribution of public offices. . . There is one matter I wish to deal with for a moment or two, and that is the fact that this government is not giving proper support to the Civil Service Commission.
Those are the words of the present Minister of Justice. Then again I have the words of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), and while I do not want to read the whole of the para,graph which I copied from Hansard some time ago, I will read one sentence. On May 2, 1921, lie said:
If there is need for consideration of any amendments to the Civil Service Act, let it be undertaken by a committee of the house formed for that particular purpose, but do not let us proceed with a series of destructive enactments in the form of a bill, everyone of which tends to weaken the scope, the authority and the usefulness of the Civil Service Commission.
Surely one cannot help wondering now that the whole cabinet are behind a bill of this kind which is absolutely contradictory to their own words, views and sentiments and, one would have thought at the time, to their action had they been in a position to put their words into effect. Instead of co-ordination and elimination, what do we find? There is a tremendous waste of time and money and many hon. members have advocated a return

National Revenue Act
to the old patronage methods. This is surprising to some of us on this side. It may be that in the past we have not had the right men on the Civil Service Commission, but before I would blame that body for all the ills existing in the public service to-day I would blame some of the shortcomings of the government in not upholding the hands of the commission in their duties. Moreover the commission undertook to direct a work that had been carried on for a number of years under perhaps the most debasing system that was prevalent in any country, the old political patronage system, which I believe was carried on to its fullest extent in this country with all its resultant work of favouritism and inefficiency. This class of appointment is the very last that should be put outside of the scope of the Civil Service Act and I am more than surprised at the Minister of National Revenue coming forward with this bill. I have looked on the debauch in the service of collecting the national revenue during these years as practically traceable to the patronage system and I am surprised that the minister himself to-day would want to assume responsibility for the appointment of those officers who perhaps are more responsible for the efficient collection of the revenue than any others.
According to the bill the Minister of National Revenue will have a board of examiners set up to determine the fitness of applicants, a board not responsible at all to parliament or in a way to himself, a board which will not be in any sense responsible for the work of the appointees. The Prime Minister, as reported on page 2847 of Hansard of May 2, 1921, used these words in a discussion on the Spinney bill:
This bill specifies three classes of appointments which are to be taken out of the hands of the Civil Service Commission and transferred to the government, thereby permitting the government's followers, in all certainty, to make recommendations which the governor in council will act upon. That is a step entirely in the wrong direction. .	. Now, Mr. Speaker,
these facts make it wholly apparent that if a measure of this kind is permitted to pass even the second reading it is setting back in a very real and substantial way the efforts of the past few years in the direction of civil service reform. .
If the whole responsibility of the civil service was on the commission, that body would at once take means to eliminate the overmanning, duplication and inefficiency. It is one of the most deplorable features of our civil service that all underlings are likely to be placed in a position that prevents any development in ability, because they are not allowed to do their best; and inefficiency must be the result. That this is the case
I have been convinced. Can anyone imagine what the detriment to the individual character must have been in the printing bureau before the last reorganization took place? From an editorial in the Toronto Globe of June 4, 1925, I gather that the sum of $744,000 was saved by that reorganization, and that economies and adjustments made in the Post Office department have affected a saving of $850,000. From the same paper, of the same date, I read these words:
If economies in the Interior department were effected similar to those in the printing bureau, as estimated by Dr. Roche, it would mean a saving of at least $1,000,000 or more a year.
Again, from another journal, a supporter of the government, I believe, the Ottawa Citizen, I read that it has been conservatively estimated that $25,000,000 could be saved by a thorough reorganization of the public service and the adoption of efficient business management. I think the average taxpayer would say that the money was needed, and was worth saving, and it could be applied to the reduction of the national debt.
From the tone of the government during the last six or seven years, one is bound to come to the conclusion that their desire is to return to the old patronage system. I should like to see the control of the civil service free entirely from party politics. There must be a connection somewhere, but in any event the Civil Service Commission should in no way be subject to the party in power, but should be composed of men who would make of the commission a body independent and responsible. A recapitulation of the facts of the last few years I think would show that our civil service is practically made subservient to partyism, and I think that the minister of National Revenue in the enactment of this bill is only creating for himself great difficulties in cleaning up his department of some abuses which we know to exist, and this bill will only make it harder still for him to get efficiency. That the civil servants who are in the customs service in Saskatchewan and Manitoba realize this is evidence I think that they see a danger ahead in this respect, and I would ask the government even at this late date to reconsider before placing an act of this kind on the statute book. I cannot but look on it as a part of a scheme to undermine the work of the Civil Service Commission. I felt that I could not let this opportunity pass and that I would not be doing my duty if I did not raise my voice in protest against such a thing.
Mr. HENRI E. LAVIGUEUR (Quebec-Montmorency) (Translation): Mr. Speaker,
National Revenue Act

if I am not mistaken this bill has for its object to amend the Act concerning the National Revenue Department so as to remedy the situation in regard to certain appointments among the higher officials in that Department. Among other things, it is stated:
"(4) The Minister may, after such examination as he may prescribe, select and nominate suitable persons for appointment by the Civil Service Commission, to positions appertaining to any of the following classes of offices,-
(a)	Customs appraisers of all classes whether serving at the various ports and places of entry or as Dominion appraisers;
(b)	All officers in the Customs-Excise preventive service;
(c)	All officers assigned to duty as investigators of values and claims for draw-back.
If such appointment is not made by the Commission within fifteen days from the date of notice to it of such selection and nomination, the Governor in Council may, on the recommendation of the Minister appoint during pleasure any such officer.
The officers so appointed by the Commission or by the Governor in Council, as the case may be, shall be paid such salaries or remuneration in accordance with civil service regulations as may be determined by the Commission or the Governor in Council respectively, and the Minister may appoint the times and manner in which the same shall be paid.
Mr. Speaker, what influenced the hon. Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Euler), to introduce this amendment to the Act concerning the National Revenue Department, was that after the famous inquiry on the administration of the Customs Department, the Commission carrying out this inquiry, recommended particularly to the government that a reorganization should be carried out.
Furthermore, such recommendations were made by the Commercial Protective Association. The minister accepted the recommendation of the Commissioners, and also those of the Association, and after giving them careful consideration, he thought fit to introduce this bill, so as to co-operate in the appointment of the higher officials in his Department. In my opinion, this does not take away from the Civil Service Commission the right of making the appointments, seeing that they are to be asked to make such appointments; but the Department would co-operate with the Commission in selecting the most capable, competent and qualified persons to fill these positions.
The Minister as well as the heads of his department are acquainted with the needs of the department; they have a knowledge of the important duties to be carried out; they certainly are in a position to advise the Civil Service Commission or the Governor in Council in regard to these appointments.

The hon. Minister of National Revenue in introducing this measure, thought it would be in the interest of both his department and the country. He informs us that it is not done with the object of bringing about political patronage; I am satisfied of this fact.
I find it strange that the leader of the opposition and his first lieutenants so strongly oppose this measure. Evidently these gentlemen do not always practice what they preach, because I remember that at the last general election, and previously, candidates of the opposition taunted us in this way: "You are in power since 1921. When we were at the helm of affairs we tried to decrease the powers of the Civil Service Commission, in 1921, by a bill introduced by one of our leaders the Hon. Mr. Spinney, and purporting to take away from this Commission, the authority of making appointments which it was not in a position to judiciously make, and you were opposed to it. You are in power since 1921 and you have kept up the Civil Service Commission. We pledge ourselves that should we be returned to power in 1926, one of the first acts of the conservative government will be to dismiss the Civil Service Commission.
I myself heard Conservative candidates make this statement and on many occasions at political meetings. To-day, the Minister of National Revenue in the interest of his department and the whole country, wishes, not to ignore the Civil Service Commission, but to co-operate with it in order to select the best officials available for his department, and this, as I have previously mentioned, to conform with the recommendations of the Commission of Inquiry and those of the Commercial Protective Association. Well, Sir, I repeat again to those who so strongly oppose this bill, that they are not sincere and consistent, since their candidates proclaimed the contrary at the last general election.
My views, Sir, as regards the Civil Service Commission are well known. I had the opportunity of referring to it many times in the house, and I shall never let the occasion slip by to state that I am absolutely opposed to that Commission.
I congratulate the hon. Minister of National Revenue who is seeking to remove a certain control and prerogative from the Civil Service Commission. I should like to see all his colleagues in the cabinet follow his good example and act in the same way for each of their departments.
Why do our hon. friends of the opposition, who are so strongly in favour of the Civil

National Revenue Act
Service Commission and taunt us when we dare criticize the Commission, not ask that all appointments be made by the Commission? Is it not a fact that all the most important appointments are made without consulting it. When it is a question of appointing a judge, it is not the Civil Service Commission that makes the selection but the government, and I believe that all such appointments have been judicious ones. When it is a question of selecting higher officials such as deputy ministers, the clerks of both houses, the Civil Service Commission has no word to say in the matter, they are appointed by the government. The same thing happens when ministers' secretaries are appointed and this procedure is followed for many other appointments.
Would our friends of the opposition approve of having all appointments made by the Civil Service Commission, even those of judges, senators and all positions pertaining to the administration of the country? Such is not my opinion and I have often stated so in this house. I think that the minister who devotes his time to the interests of his department and makes a complete and serious study of it, is better qualified than the Civil Service Commission to select the best officials for his department.
I feel confident, Sir, that the house will approve the request of the hon. minister of National Revenue and will support the measure which I consider of the utmost importance and in the interest of the whole country. I shall therefore give it my entire support.

Mr. Speaker, I have an amendment to offer, seconded by Mr. Irvine, as follows:

I
rise to a point of order. The amendment is not in order as no notice has been given. According to the rules, notice of motion must be given beforehand.

Standing order 113 reads as follows:
No important amendment may be proposed to any private bill, in a committee of the whole house, or at the third reading of the bill, unless one day's notice of the same has been given.
Has notice of this amendment been given?

I declare the amendment out of order.
The member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church) cannot now move another amendment. He has exercised his right to speak on the third reading in moving the amendment which has been declared out of order.
There may be other amendments to which the hon. gentleman can speak later on.

In many respects I regret that I find it necessary to oppose the bill before the house. The chief reason why I regret it is I believe that the hon. gentleman who is sponsoring it has overlooked certain things in regard to it. His position in the house is not doubted by anyone, and I believe he is sincere and has the good of the public at heart. But while this bill was before the committee of the whole the hon. gentleman's actions were not the best that might have been hoped for. Such a bill as this involves the public interest to a very large extent, and should be discussed fully. I question very much whether it ought to be passed at all, but certainly it
fMr. Dickie.]

Bell Telephone Company
should not be passed in its present form. There are amendments which should be introduced, and which should have been moved in the committee of the w'hole where they could have been discussed thoroughly.
We in this corner of the house have been accused of talking the bill out. I want to dissociate myself from that insinuation. I think that hon. members should be free to offer any criticism which they feel should be made regarding any bill, without the imputation that they are adopting blocking tactics. Personally I have no interest at all in talking out this or any other bill, but certain things in connection with the public interest apply to this bill which I think should be fully discussed on the floor of this house.
When the hon. gentleman moved in the committee of the whole that this bill be reported, I do not think that was good tactics. One of Disraeli's biographers, in discussing Mr. Gladstone, said that people did not object to Mr. Gladstone so much because he usually had a trump card up his sleeve which he applied at the proper time, but they objected because he usually said that the trump card had been placed there at his disposal by Providence. I do not object to the hon. gentleman playing this trump card which he had up his sleeve, but when it is argued that such trump card is in the best interests of legislation, and the best interests of the country, I very much doubt it.
We are passing, Mr. Speaker, gradually from the old competitive system. The competitive system is yielding to great mergers and combines. When this system was at its height we had competition in services and competition in prices, which was an effective check upon overcharges. I do not wish to return to that old system where we had numerous small businesses trying to compete with each other; I think that day is well past. However, competition did check exorbitant charges, and since competition has yielded to large mergers, interlocking directorates, subsidiary companies, and so forth, there must be substituted some check to take the place of the competitive method which governed charges in the past. We have passed into a condition where monopolies are prevalent.
The company involved in the present bill is virtually a monopoly. The Bell Telephone Company is, I believe, controlled very largely by the American Telephone & Telegraph Company. In turn the Bell Telephone Company controls the subsidiary company from which it receives a great part if not all of its supplies. That subsidiary company practically controls the supply of all the supplies for
the telephone service, so that this monopoly, unless the government takes some definite action to control it, is left uncontrolled.
It is public knowledge that less than a year ago the railway commission, on the request of the company in question, increased the telephone rates in Ontario and Quebec. Those telephone rates were increased so that those provinces had to pay what might be regarded as a tax of some $2,600,000 extra last year for telephone service. I understand that the railway commission, when the rate question was before it, refused to allow representatives of the various provinces to present the case of those provinces, and the increase was granted. I presume it was granted on the grounds as presented by the company, namely, that their overhead and so forth warranted them in asking for the right to make higher charges, and I think it will not be difficult to see that if the present capital increase is granted the company will have a greater ground to ask for still further increases.
Let me come to the bill itself and the chief points in respect of which I wish to raise objection. The bill proposes to increase the capitalization of the company by $75,000,000. In this connection let me remind the house that the act incorporating the company was a special statute according to which the company must, if required, submit to investigation. We have a right to investigate that company as to how it has previously disposed of its stock. We have a right to know to whom the stock was sold, how much was paid for it and what was done with the proceeds. These questions in a utility of this kind, the profits of which are practically guaranteed by the public, should be thoroughly investigated. I suggest to the house that an increase of $75,000,000 in capitalization should not be authorized by parliament until a thorough investigation has been made into the company's history of stock selling. I believe at the present time the company has some $12,000,000 of unissued stock. It may be argued and argued successfully that a large company of this kind may have a legitimate right to ask for an increase of $75,000,000 in capitalization, but when we look at the facts we will begin to doubt whether or not this is so. In the past the company has had the habit of issuing its stock to its own shareholders at the par value of $100, while the market value has been ranging from $125 to $193. It can be readily seen that a much smaller issue of stock than $75,000,000 would bring into the coffers of the company the same amount of money that would be brought in by its past methods of issuing stock, so that we ought to be assured that the stock will not be issued to the shareholders of the company in this manner, but that it will be
Bell Telephone Company

left open to be purchased by the public in general. That is one of the amendments which should be passed if this bill is to go through parliament and now we have no opportunity even to move it. That is one reason why I wish to protest against the methods which were adopted in putting this bill through the house. In respect to what I have just said, I wish to quote a very short extract from an article in the Toronto Globe, written by Mr. Reid, who I believe was counsel for the province of Ontario before the railway commission when the matter of telephone rates was up for discussion a short time ago. He says:
The history of its stock issues shows that the company has been making a regular practice of issuing stock to its shareholders at par of $100 per share 'when it was listed and selling on the exchanges at market prices, forty per cent, fifty per cent, sixty per cent, seventy-five per cent, and in one instance in the year 1899 at ninety-three per cent higher than its ar value, and in each of such cases the share-olders were given a bonus of $40, $47, $50, $60, $75 and $93 per share, in addition to the regular dividend of eight per cent.
Parliament has a right to safeguard the public against the continuation of this practice. If the company really require $75,000,000 increase in capital we should know in the public interest whether that sum of $75,000,000 is to be divided out to its own shareholders at a par value of $100, when the stock is worth $193. If parliament allows the bill to pass without safeguarding the public in that respect, it will be remiss in its duty. It is clear to everybody that the dividends must be paid on the stock issue, and if dividends are to be paid on $75,000,000 worth of stock that may not be required, where are the dividends to come from? The dividends can come only from the telephone charges, so that if the telephone charges are not sufficiently high now to afford such dividends, another appeal will be made to the Board of Railway Commissioners for an increase and thus we shall be placing a still greater burden upon the users of the telephone system.
Let me come to the second point to which I object in respect to the bill. I have referred already to its subsidiary company the Northern Electric Company. This Company sells practically all the supplies which the Bell Telephone Company require. I am given to understand that it is possible-and perhaps there is more than a suggestion that this is being done- that in purchasing supplies from its own subsidiary company the Bell Telephone Company may pay a much higher price than it ought to pay were it buying at a fair market value. Thus it reduces the profits which will appear on the books of the Bell Telephone Company

and gives an excuse for increasing the rates, although meanwhile it is taking in its profits by means of the subsidiary company. With regard to the subsidiary let me remark that the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Geary) has before the house a bill which will grant the right to investigate telephone subsidiary companies. For some strange reason or another that bill is now under public bills and orders and it will not be reached this session, but if the bill under discussion is to become law, the bill to which I have referred should also foe passed this session. We ought to have a right to investigate the subsidiary companies in order to make sure that none of this sort of practice is going on, or, if it is going on, that it should immediately cease. But if we sit quietly by while a bill of this character is railroaded through parliament, what opportunity have we, as representatives of the public, to safeguard their interests in this respect? If the bill is to be proceeded with, we have a right to ask the government to guarantee to us that the bill to which I have referred shall be placed before parliament this session and that we shall have an opportunity to deal with it.
With regard' to the extravagant prices which are alleged to have been charged by the subsidiary company, I wish to quote a paragraph or two from an editorial in the Toronto Globe:
If the relations between the Northern Electric and Bell Telephone companies are such that the rates which the Bell Company charges are used in part to enhance unduly the returns of the former, telephone users are entitled to protection from the railway board. The public has sanctioned the operation of the Bell as a monopoly and is guaranteeing its dividends, and has a right to know whether it is paying its money for service, or also for the support of a subsidiary on which there is no cheek.
Further it says:
The public wants to know, first, why the vast amounts of materials which the Bell Company purchases come from the one source, and whether the conditions imposed are such that there can be little or no competition.
In this connection I desire to point out that it is alleged that the subsidiary company makes a practice of selling its old, secondhand, worn out goods to the Bell Telephone Company at first class prices. That is another method by which it is alleged this company may cover up its profits. I believe also that the western provinces, although they control publicly their telephone service, are practically compelled to buy from this subsidiary company of the Bell Telephone Company, and the charges of the publicly-owned telephones are consequently made higher through these overcharges.

Bell Telephone Company
I do not wish further to delay the business of the house. I think that my hon. friend will not charge me with trying to talk out this bill. I have placed before the house the two main points of objection I have to this bill: First, that the method of the company in issuing its stock is not sound, that it issues stock to its own shareholders at a par value of $100 when the value of the stock on the market is much higher, and in so doing not only slices a melon amongst its shareholders, but increases the charges for telephone service in order to pay dividends on unnecessary capital. Second, I say that the subsidiary company, the Northern Electric Company, is controlled by the Bell Telephone Company, and in selling its supplies to the Bell Telephone Company may overcharge, and thus excuse the company for seeking higher rates for telephone service. For these reasons I say that this bill should either be defeated entirely by parliament, or be so amended as to safeguard the public in the respects to which I have referred.

solve this problem by granting to the Board of Railway Commissioners the right to investigate such companies as the Northern Electric Company and determine whether or not the Bell Telephone Company is entitled to any consideration. I quote again from the letter to which I referred:
Professor Lamar Lyndon, one of the finest public utility experts in the United States, in his work on public utilities says: "The interrelationships of the local Bell companies with some district organization and of the district organization with the American Telegraph and Telephone Company make it almost impossible to determine true costs and overhead charges for a local exchange.

The Western Electric Company manufactures all the material used by the Bell Telephone Company in the United States, and is practically the only source of supply.
Let me take a moment to consider the Northern Electric Company in Canada. Fifty per cent of the stock of that company is held by the Bell Telephone Company, 6 per cent or more by the directors of the Bell Telephone Company and the balance by the Western Electric Company in the United States. The Western Electric Company, in turn, is owned by the American Telegraph and Telephone Company, which owns the Bell Telephone Company and so on, so everything paid into the treasury goes to this company in the United States. Of course, to be fair I must say that that would not apply to any shares held in Canada, but these are comparatively few because the stock is controlled as I have outlined. This latter company was organized, financed, and built up with the money, property and assets of the Bell Telephone Company. The policy appears to have been to keep the profits of the Bell Telephone Company at the very minimum, so that in appearing before the Board of Railway Commissioners the company would find no difficulty in obtaining authority to increase its rates. In that way they could hide their profits and keep them hidden indefinitely. This could be easily carried to a point where the Bell Telephone Company would show no profits at all, and even if we increased rates it could be still carried on so that no profits would be shown. That is, they could pay more for their equipment secured from the Northern Electric Company, leave all the profits there and get them by indirect means. Of course I do not say that that will be done, but unless something is done to prevent it that remains possible. Again I quote from this letter:
All this is done and is aided by hiding behind a 25 to 30 per cent tariff wall on telephone apparatus and equipment. It would still remain a monopoly without any tariff, and yet prevent the duty being added to the price. The government telephone services of the three provinces of western Canada are all tied by this same yoke.
That is where I have a very direct interest. It might be easily said that the Bell Telephone Company operates only in Ontario and Quebec and that this increase in rates affects only the people of those provinces, but I say that in a larger way this whole question which is opened up by the discussion of any concessions granted to the Bell Telephone Company does very materially affect the interests of the people of western Canada. Fortunately we have publicly owned telephone systems in those three provinces, of which we are proud; these systems are owned and controlled by the people and are giving splendid service. But, sir, of what avail is this to us when we find that the source from which we must obtain all our supplies is controlled by the Bell Telephone Company of eastern Canada? By raising the price they can make us pay whatever they wish for the use of our telephones in those three provinces, because they enjoy what is a monopoly in supplying telephone equipment in this country. In 1925 the Northern Electric Company sold $12,000,000 worth of supplies to the Bell Telephone Company. There is very little doubt that excessive prices were charged for these supplies to leave a profit in the hands of the Northern Electric Company rather than in the hands of the Bell Telephone Company. At the end of 1925, the Northern Electric Company had a reserve and surplus of $8,409,000, where the total value of the prop-

Bell Telephone Company
erty and plant was only $9,882,000; the surplus and reserve being almost equal to the entire value of their plant. I will quote from this newspaper again:
If we take the depreciation reserve alone for 1925, it is over 100 per cent, and nearly 125 per cent of the plant. For the year 1924 the depreciation reserve represented 100 per cent of the plant and equipment. For the year 1923 it was also over 100 per cent, for 1922 it was also 100 per cent, for 1921 it was also 100 per cent depreciation reserve in relation to their plant, while for the year 1920 the depreciation reserve represented 129 per cent of their plant and equipment.
This looks very much like the old scriptural tale of turning water into wine, only in this case it is turning water into gold. All these surpluses have been built up from profits and earniings made by the company, and contributions made to that end not by the security holders but by those who patronised the company; they have all been built up by profits made in the operation of the company.
On December 31, 1925, the statement of the Northern Electric Company showed a building and real estate surplus of $5,388,000; depreciation reserve of $5,564,000, and an undivided surplus of $2,844,000, nearly all of which was earned from the users of the Bell Telephone Company. There is nothing at all to prevent the Bell Telephone Company from earning no profits at all, allowing this to be done by the subsidiaries to such an extent that the original company would show no profit. If we permit this sort of thing to continue there will be an excuse for a regularly increasing scale of rates, which will have to be paid by the people of these provinces.
I would like to quote further from this letter. This particular paragraph refers to the question of giving the Board of Railway Commissioners power to investigate the subsidiary company, the Northern Electric Company. It reads as follows:
And that is just what we are going to do, with the help and assistance of the bill now before the parliament of Canada, and in this connection I may say that the United States senate recently ordered an investigation of this very same nature to be gone on with, and the city of Boston, and a number of other large centres have filed printed indictments and complaints with the Interstate Commerce Commission at Washington, asking for a United States-wide inquiry of these same matters for which the parliament of Canada is now being asked to pass a bill in order to commence a similar investigation in Canada.
The bill that we are now discussing provides for a new stock issue. This would be perfectly all right if the company sold its stock on the market and put the proceeds into its treasury to be used in the extension of its service, but we have no guarantee that this is 56103-1961
not just a means of hiding further profit. We have no right to pass this bill until such time as the operations of this company and its subsidiaries are thoroughly investigated. On December 31, 1925, the depreciation reserve of the Bell Telephone Company amounted to $23,295,000, and the surplus to $6,800,000-this in addition to the fact that a lot of their earnings have been withheld from them. In spite of that, we still find the company with this very comfortable surplus of nearly $30,000,000, all of which is built up not by the investment of the security holders, but by the tolls paid by the users of telephones in Ontario and Quebec.
We propose by this bill to give the company the right to capitalize their surplus, or what is ordinarily called stock watering. We propose to allow them to issue stock bonuses against this surplus, and allow them to capitalize it. I do not say that they will do so but the users of the telephones might easily ibe in the position of being compelled to pay dividends on the very surplus which their contributions to the company have created.
Western Canada, as I said, is indirectly interested in this whole thing, because we buy our supplies from the same source. This is the most barefaced piece of villany and imposition ever attempted upon a free people, and its exposure before this honourable board will not be the last this corporate monopoly will hear about it.
This is not something that has come from the so-called radical farmer governments of the west; this is not a public statement by the hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Evans), but it is a statement of the representative of the Conservative government of Ontario before

the Board of Railway Commissioners. The people of that province protested against an increase in rates, but it was put through in spite of that. speechtext:
I do not wish to take the time of the house to any great length. I am in favour of this bill, and I believe that the increase in capitalization asked for by the Bell Telephone Company is necessary in order that they may carry out and perform an efficient public service. At the present time they are under the control of the Board of Railway Commissioners. Their profits from telephone service are regulated by that board; their dividends upon their capital stock are, in a like manner, regulated. The basis of that regulation is that every $100 of capital stock shall be represented by $190 cash paid into the treasury of the company. That is secured by the bill in the form in which it is now presented to the house, and if the company is earning from its telephonic service as a public utility a larger rate of dividend than should be paid on a share of stock which represents $100 in cash, that is a matter which can and which will be from time to time regulated by the Board of Railway Commissioners.
I do not intend to discuss at the present time another bill 'before the house which would give to the Board of Railway Commissioners the power of investigating subsidiary companies. When that bill comes before the house I shall be prepared to discuss it. I do not believe in making invidious distinctions in such matters, and if the act constituting the Board of Railway Commissioners is to be amended, let us deal fairly with all public utilities coming before that board and let us make the same provision apply to all public utility companies. I see that grave distinctions may be drawn. I do not see why freight rates over the national railway system should depend upon the amount that its subsidiary companies, hotel companies, are earning. I do not see why freight rates on Canadian Pacific railway should be governed by the amount of profit on the Canadian Pacific steamship lines. There are such considerations which must receive from the house

due attention when it has before it that other bill to which reference has been made, which was introduced by the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Geary) and which, I have no doubt, will receive fair and adequate consideration by the house. But an increase in the capital of the Bell Telephone Company is in my opinion absolutely necessary in order that it may perform the public service which it has undertaken to perform, which the public are demanding should be performed in the way of extensions to its lines and to its business.
The matter of the relation of the Northern Electric Company to the Bell Telephone Company came before the Board of Railway Commissioners in 1921 and I will read just a very short extract from the decision of that board under date of April 1, 1921. The board said as to the relation of the Northern Electric Company to the Bell Telephone Company- and I am reading from the decision of the commissioner who gave the judgment:
As the matter presents itself to me, this is a phase of company management into which the board is not authorized to go. What the board is concerned with in the public interest is to see that reasonable prices have been charged, this having a necessary bearing on the question of the position from a net revenue standpoint of the company purchasing materials.
On consideration of the evidence, and bearing in mind the supplementary comparative material as to prices which the board has obtained, and which is referred to in an earlier connection, I am of the opinion that it has not been shown that the prices charged are unreasonable.
That is, the prices charged on the material purchased by the Bell Telephone Company from the Northern Electric Company. I am not going to follow the various judgments down to the present time, but I will call attention for a moment to an extract from the majority judgment of the Board of Railway Commissioners rendered on February 21, 1927. I prefer that majority judgment to the rather extravagant assertions of counsel 'for any authority who appeared before the board. At least, after the commissioners had heard the arguments of counsel, this was the considered judgment of a majority of the board:
It has been established that the prices charged by the Northern Electric Company, under the most favoured customer's clause, were lower than those which the Bell Telephone Company would have been obliged to pay to other manufacturers.
It also appears obvious that the Northern Electric Company is able, on account of its mass production and volume of trade, to manufacture and sell at a lower cost than the Bell Telephone Company could manufacture or purchase if it were limited only to its own requirements.
There is no evidence of any improper financial arrangements between the two companies,

Bell Telephone Company
and the agreement and the supplementary agreement which govern their relations are distinctly advantageous to the Bell Telephone Company.
The board can be concerned only with the effect of the Bell Telephone Company's purchase of materials, from the standpoint of its net revenue.
On consideration of the evidence, one is compelled to reach the conclusion that it has not been shown that the prices charged were unreasonable; on the contrary, it was shown that such prices were as low or lower than those charged to other customers.
In view of that considered judgment I think the house should not commingle the two considerations.
Mr. DUNNING; That is the point. I was just about to raise a point of order on the very matter that my hon. friend is now mentioning, because we are in danger of drifting into a debate, precipitated by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell), on another bill which is on the order paper, and I am sure my hon. friend does not desire that.

No. I am simply returning to the consideration that in view of that considered judgment the house, with due respect to the judgment of its own court, should now eliminate all questions as to the purchase of materials, because those can and will be dealt with from time to time under other statutes. Therefore we have to come back to the consideration of the merits of the bill. This increase of capital is necessary. It was proved to be necessary to the satisfaction of the railway committee of this house and the bill was reported unanimously, if I remember correctly, by that committee. It has been considered and it has been reported by the committee of the whole house by a very large majority. Under those circumstances I do not intend to take further time to justify my position in voting wholeheartedly for the measure.

Before the hon. member
sits down, would he make a little clearer the point to which he referred in the beginning of his speech when he said that it was provided in the bill itself that for every $100 share, $100 should go to the treasury of the company.

Under the Bell Telephone
Company's acts of incorporation as they are amended down to the present time the stock can be issued only for cash. There are in those acts of incorporation no such provisions as we have seen in some recent bills before the house for the issue of stock for other considerations.
I ask that question because the objection has been raised that in this particular bill that is not made clear.
The whole scope of the act renders it impossible to issue stock for other considerations than cash.
Is the house ready for the question?

I was under the impression, Mr. Speaker, that the sponsor of the bill was about to answer some of the arguments that have been levelled from this part of the house at the bill.
In the first place, let me say very definitely that I have examined at considerable length this bill and the affairs of both companies on which discussion has taken place, and I am not yet convinced that the increase in capital asked for is at all needed. I will give my reason for that in a sentence. At the present time the Bell Telephone Company has power to add to its capital to the extent of $48,000,000 without issuing one dollar's worth of new stock. It can increase its capital by $48,000,000 without any amendment to its original charter. The stock capital issued is about $62,000,000, and there is still allowed to be issued under the original charter about $13,000,000. The bond issue is $40,000,000. So the company can issue in bonds around $35,000,000 more, and $13,000,000 of stock, or a total of $48,000,000. Would that be good business? Is it good business for a corporation of this kind to carry fifty per cent of its capital in stock and fifty per cent in bonds? There is no question as to the opinion of authorities on that point; they are agreed that it is good policy. The company have even admitted that is good policy before the board of railway commissioners. So here you have a company that at the present moment has power to increase its capital by $48,000,000 coming to parliament and asking for the right to increase its stock capital by the amount of $75,000,000 more before it has exhausted its power in respect of the original capital by $48,000,000.
Let the house not forget this fact that every $100 share of capital stock carries eight per cent interest. That eight per cent is absolutely guaranteed by the Board of Railway Commissioners. It the company's earnings are less than eight per cent, all that it has to do is to make an application to the Board of Railway Commissioners and prove that it is not earning enough to pay eight per cent with the present rates for service, and immediately those rates are increased. So the effect of the whole regulations under which
Bell Telephone Company

this semi-public utility is operated is to guarantee to the shareholders of the company eight per cent on their stock. But the bonds carry only five per cent. Now I ask any hon. gentleman a simple question:	Will it be
better for the users of telephones in this country that the interest charges on the capital shall be five per cent or eight per cent? Obviously the rates must be higher the more stock that is out at eight per cent, than if that capital were out at five per cent. That is clear. Of course, another question may arise as to the proper use of bonds and stock, but that is not yet an important factor because the company has not yet brought its bond issue to the same amount as its capital stock issue.
Let us examine the company in some detail for a few years back, and find out what has been the percentage issued in bonds and stock:
