It will be clear to the house that the company is rapidly coming to the point where the balance between the bonds and stock issued would, in the opinion of experts, be just about right for a company of this kind. Why then, should1 this house now increase the capital stock by $75,000,000, on which the company will have to pay eight per cent interest, thus increasing the overhead charges on the operations of the company, possibly leading to a further increase in the charges to the users of the service later oh.
There is a principle involved in this whole business to which the house should in my opinion direct attention, and that is whether we are going to permit any longer public utility corporations whose earnings are guaranteed, whose interest is guaranteed, whose cost of operation is guaranteed by the rates which they are permitted to charge under a monopoly, to issue stock to its own shareholders, who are now making excellent dividends, at present rates. A rate of eight per cent is not a rate to shut your eyes to. In addition to that, how long are we going to allow them to take from the users of telephones, gifts through the stock being issued to the shareholders at a lower price than the market price of the stock to-day? Let me give an illustration of what I mean. If this

bill passes, there at once becomes available a stock issue of $10,000,000. The shareholders can buy that stock at $100 per share, and under the present market valuation it is worth $172.50. So the shareholders-and this privilege of buying the stock at $100 per share is restricted to the present shareholders -by virtue of this first claim on the stock get not only $100 worth of stock earning eight per cent interest, but a gift of $72.50 as well.
Provided the market holds.

It may be said at once that the market will not hold. I grant you that if you offer this stock for public subscription, the market will not hold. What will happen will be that the stock may slump to some degree, but immediately if the stock were offered to public subscription the coffers of the company would be benefited by $50 to $60 a share more than if the stock were issued at par to the private shareholders of the company. That is a principle which this house sooner or later will have to consider seriously with a view to amending the charters under which all such companies operate, in order to prevent the issuing of stock to its own shareholders at par. All the stock of companies of this kind should be sold at open auction, so that it can get out on the markets of the world. If that were done in the case of every company whose interest and earnings are guaranteed, there would be a greater return to the treasury of the company than there is under the present system of issuing stock.
Recently, as has been pointed out, the rates of the Bell Telephone Company were increased in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec to an extent that simply meant an additional burden of taxation upon the telephone users to the amount of $2,600,000 a year. I venture to assert that if the stock of the Bell Telephone Company had been selling on the open markets since the outset, there would not have been the necessity for this increase of rates, because there would have been more money in the company carrying a lower rate of interest if bonds were issued, and certainly there would be more money in the company if the stock had been sold at the market price instead of at the par value of $100. This application of the Bell Telephone Company for increased rates, which was acceded to by the Board of Railway Commissioners to the extent to which I have stated, was made really by the American Telephone and Telegraph Company of New York, but through, of course, the Bell Tele-

Bell Telephone Company
phone Company of Canada, which, it controls.
I am informed that the Board of Railway Commissioners definitely refused the people of Ontario and Quebec the right to argue their case in person, and that this attitude of the board was upheld, on appeal, by the government. Here is a condition of affairs, again, to which public attention should be directed. Here is a situation to which the public cannot be blind. Here was an application by a public utility company in which the public are very much concerned, and yet the public were denied the right to present their case in person.
It was conclusively proven at the same hearing to which I have referred that the Bell Telephone Company did issue its stock at par, $100 per share, to its shareholders. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) is quite correct in stating that the stock was sold for $100 in cash, or its equivalent, and that that actually went into the coffers of the company; but the hon. gentleman did not add that in every case of stock issue that has come to my attention there has also been a gift, depending on the market price of the stock, ranging from $23 to $93 per share. In every case of that kind a part, if not all, of the increment should have gone into the treasury of the company, and so have prevented an unnecessary issue of stock. Hon. members do not require to examine into this procedure very far to see that if the company wants $15,000,000 of stock for development purposes, they can sell their stock at $150 on the market, and will not have to issue as much of it as if they were selling it to their own shareholders at $100 per share. In that way you keep down the fixed charges because of the lesser quantity of stock issued.
Under the present stock issue to the shareholders of the company, if it was all issued at the market valuation of to-day it would mean a gift direct to the shareholders^ of several million dollars, off the bat. That is a pretty nice little gift. In my opinion no public utility company should be allowed to do this. Its stock should not be available as a gift to the shareholders; it should be sold on the open market. Moreover, as I have said, less stock would be required if the company was obliged to sell it on the open market. This form of stock issue amounts to stock bonusing, although not by a direct stock bonus issue. It was largely because of this method of keeping the increment for the privileged shareholders that a larger stock issue became necessary than would otherwise have been the case, always followed, of course,
by a corresponding straining of the earnings to meet the dividends on the increased quantity of stock outstanding. It is therefore quite apparent, Mr. Speaker, that so long as this company is permitted to make presents of its increment of stock to its shareholders there will be maintained as high, or even higher, rates than are now charged the users of telephones. Inevitably in the long run the telephone subscribers must pay for these periodical gifts to the stockholders.
This is a special form of legalized brigandage of the highest order. The other day my attention was called to a press despatch from New York, from which I learned that some four or five men had raided a candy factory and made away with $7,500, if I remember correctly, but the pursuit of the police was too close and the alleged bandits abandoned their car and their booty. The police continued their chase and left the car standing in the road. The nice, good men in the street promptly helped themselves to the money, and when the police got back to the car there was only $200 left. In my opinion as between the two types of thieves, the man who frankly went out and faced society as his enemy and took his chance was more courageous and of as high moral standing as the sneak who stole the money from the car. So I say, Mr. Speaker, that members of the community in Canada or in other country who continue to steal, from the users of telephones, gifts in the way of stock issues of this kind are as much brigands-although within the law unfortunately- as the men who entered the car and helped themselves to what had already been stolen by' somebody else. The sooner this sort of thing is stopped the better it is going to be for the country. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I now move:
That the said bill be not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole for the purpose of amending it by adding the following section:
3. No issue of the capital stock of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada shall be made except by way of offering the same to the public for subscription.
Hon. members will notice that I am not giving the bill the six months' hoist, I am not attempting to block its passage. All I am asking is that the stock be made available to the public for subscription, instead of apportioning the stock to the shareholders at par when it has a value of $170 on the open market. It is a fair proposal, and I feel satisfied that the thinking element in this House will support it. I feel satisfied that hon. gentlemen who have the public interest at heart, and who believe in the interest of
Bell Telephone Company

the consumers rather than in the interest of the shareholders will support my proposal.
There is nothing further I can say on this matter, Mr. Speaker, except to urge that is would have been much wiser altogether for this house to have delayed the third reading of this bill until after we had dealt with the other bill that is on the order paper in the name of the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Geary). The .hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) a moment ago was afraid that there might .be introduced into this debate another and entirely foreign issue. Into the merits of his objection I need not now enter. All I wish to say is that the two bills are absolutely inter-related; one inevitably affects the other. Whether this house would in its wisdom pass the Bell Telephone bill after we had sanctioned the bill of the member for South Toronto is a very serious question in my mind. I do not believe the house would pass the Bell Telephone bill until the railway commission had had an opportunity of investigating the affairs of the Northern Electric Company.
I cannot agree with all that has been said by one or two members that have preceded me with respect to the profits that may have been made by the Northern Electric Company from the sale of standard goods supplied to the Bell Telephone Company. I have studied the evidence in the matter, and I agree with a statement made by the hon. member from St. Lawrence-St. George. It has not been brought to my attention at least that there have been any excessive charges by the Northern Electric Company. But the principle of the thing is what interests me. It is wrong in my opinion that a subsidiary should be allowed the possibility of milking a parent company. That is what I object to. I wish to direct the attention of the Minister of Railways to a statement in a report of the Public Service Commission of Virginia. In 1922 that commission had occasion to deal with this very question and an order was made directing disclosure of the factory and production costs and profits of two companies affected, and ordering them to prove that the public was not being imposed upon. The commission in its judgment said:
To hold otherwise would be to hold that the American Telephone and Telegraph Company, a public service corporation, having obtained practically a monopoly of the telephone industry, may charter the Western Electric Company, a non-public service corporation, own 98 per cent of its stock, absolutely control its operation, policies and charges, and use it with impunity as a milkman to milk the funds of its local operating companies (which are public service corporations) into its own pail, without any possibility of control or restraint from this 
commission or any other governmental body, regardless of the extent to which the milking process might be carried.
Just in passing I would direct, as I say, his attention to statements of other commissions.

If my hon. friend will permit me a question for my own information: He surely does not suggest that the same conditions apply in Canada, under the present law in relation to the railway commission, as are there depicted by the West Virginia body?

I will answer the question by saying this: The Northern Electric Company in Canada has virtually a monopoly of the handling of standard telephone equipment. Yes, they have. The hon. member shakes his head, but he is absolutely incorrect.

I have merely the experience of having been Minister of Telephones in my own province and of having bought equipment elsewhere than from the Northern Electric, having been able to get it in competition with them.

My hon.
friend is incorrect. The Northern Electric has a virtual monopoly-those were the words I used-in this country, because of the nature of its standard equipment. I have a very vivid recollection of an attempt made not long ago by a British telephone manufacturing company to invade this country and set up in business. First of all it had to climb over a tariff wall of from 20 to 27^ per cent, and after it got here it had to face the concentrated efforts of this one great corporation which has practically a monopoly of standard telephone equipment in North America-in Canada certainly. That being the case, and inasmuch as the directors of the Northern Electric are the same men who are on the directorate of the Bell Telephone Company, does the minister mean to assert for a moment that it is beyond the bounds of possibility that these directors would milk the subsidiary Bell Telephone Company for the good of the shareholders of the Northern Electric? An hon. gentleman suggests that it is the other way around; it might be. The minister has too much knowledge of modern commercial practice to assert that it is not possible for them to do this. It is a common practice to-day, and the reports of commissions which I have will testify to it. I have given one. It may not be an absolute analogy but it is of the type of practice to which I have referred.

Bell Telephone Company
I do not wish unduly to delay this bill going to a vote, and I will conclude with this remark. It is my sincere hope that hon. gentlemen opposite who in the past have joined with us in our opposition to the undue inflation of stock and to the unfair milking of the consumer will now support a simple amendment of this kind. It does not prevent the bill from being passed; it does not prevent the bill going through and the company getting the increase in capital. All it provides is that future stock issues must be made available for public subscription and not be given in part as gifts to private individuals.

If much that has been said, and a great deal more that has been implied, regarding the Bell Telephone Company were accurate I should feel fully persuaded to resist this bill with all the vigour that has characterized the speech of my hon. friend from Bow River (Mr. Garland), who has just taken his seat. If the directorate of the Bell Telephone Company and the directorate of the Northern Electric were brigands and pirates-I believe that was the term used-then of course parliament ought properly to be alarmed at a bill of this character. I think however that possibly it was the anxiety of my hon. friend from Bow River to impress his views upon the house that led him to indulge in rather strenuous language in his expression of those views. The hon. gentleman is possessed of a degree of facility of speech which in my opinion made unnecessary the extreme statements to which he resorted.

I would remind the hon. member that counsel for Ontario, before the board, used language just as strong.
Mr. STEVENlS:	I heard some language
read, emanating from an apparently very able legal representative before the railway board, and I must say I was mildly surprised, to say the least, at the vigour of it. I confess to having indulged in a similar practice myself occasionally, and I realize that when you have a rather weak case you can sometimes conceal its weakness by injecting into your language a little more mustard, shall I say, than perhaps would otherwise be necessary. I am free to say that it is with no great degree of pride that I look back upon those occasions upon which I have had recourse to this practice. And now that we are in this happy frame of mind, I may observe that the finest speech I ever made in my life, out of the few thousands that I have made, was of about five minutes' duration and of a character entirely different from that which I am now describing.

I will try to do so, and I hope it will be as effective. There are a few points which I think the house might keep in mind in considering this question. In the first place, this is a public utility company, and under the statutes incorporating the company parliament has placed it, in so far as its rates and its dealings with the public are concerned, under the control and direction of the Board of Railway Commissioners. In all matters appertaining to its dealings with the public this company must submit itself to the railway board.
I propound to the house this question : Are we to accept the decisions of the railway board only when such decisions meet with our peculiar and particular views, whatever they may be? Let me make a slight personal reference by way of illustration. For many years I had the firm conviction that certain railway rates were inequitable and unfair, and yet those railway rates were on several occasions maintained by the railway board. It does not follow that you must refrain from appealing, logically, legally and reasonably, to the board to secure redress. That does not follow. But it does follow, I think, that we ought not in some other place to attack or discredit the decisions of the board. So far as this question is concerned, therefore, I take this position, that the railway board having dealt fully and carefully with this company in the matter of rates, I accept their decision,
In the second place, the railway board determined that it was fair to permit this company to earn 8 per cent on its investment For the moment that is not in question. It might be a proper thing to say that their finding in that regard was unfair to the public, and to go before the board and say, " We believe it should be 6 per cent or 5 per cent " That is a reasonable position to take. But I do not think that we should say that the company constitutes a form of brigandage which is " milking " from the public unfair earnings, so long as it keeps within the decision of the board.
Another question has arisen, the question of the market price of stock. I wish to say one or two words on that point. It has 'been stated that the present market price of this stock is $165 or $170; I do not know whether or not that is correct but it will do for the purposes of argument. It is said that the price being $165 or $170, this stock therefore, Should be issued only at that rate. What fixes the market value of stocks? There are two main factors, first the earning power of the stock, and then the value of money
Bell Telephone Company

in the money markets of the world. When money is being loaned at the rate of 4 per cent, when prime securities are earning 4 per cent in the money markets of the world, a stock with a fixed earning power of 8 per cent will sell at a good deal more than par value. That is Obvious. If in the course of a few months or a few days the money markets change, as they did a few years ago when government securities rose to 5i per cent or 6 per cent, that stock with a fixed earning of 8 per cent will drop correspondingly. So it will go up and down, not particularly because of the condition of the company but because of the value of money in the markets of the world, which will regulate to a large degree the price of that stock which has a fixed earning power of 8 per cent.
There is another point to be considered; there is the element of risk to the owners of this stock in regard to earnings. Someone described this as a guaranteed stock. Dt is not guaranteed at all; it is a stock upon which the railway board have said they will permit earnings up to 8 per cent. Let us assume that a period of depression sweeps over the country and a large number of people give up their telephone service, which naturally follows during a depression. In such a case the earnings of the company might fall; that might be reasonably expected, and the earnings upon the stock would fall correspondingly. The owners of the stock take that risk of a drop in the earnings of the company. It is true that at present Canada is a young and growing country and that this company is constantly expanding, but it is not unreasonable to expect that during some period in these alternate cycles of prosperity and depression the earnings of the company may fall much 'below 8 per cent.
Then would they not immediately ask for an increase in the rates?

Possibly they would, and in such a case the railway board would take the whole situation into consideration and would determine as a judicial body whether or not that application should be granted. I think that is not a question with which parliament should concern itself. Seeing that the question has been raised, although it is not our business, perhaps we are justified in asking whether the rates are unreasonable. 1 have already said that we are not the body to determine that point; the Board of Railway Commissioners say the rates are reasonable, and I understand that they have in-

creased these rates within the last year. Perhaps it is interesting to note that the rates paid in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec where the chief operations of the Bell Telephone Company centre are lower than those charged by any other telephone system in this country. That is worthy of being taken into consideration. I do not offer that fact as evidence that rates are fair, because the Board of Railway Commissioners have determined that point, but I do say that it is evidence that the rates are not highly unfair; it is evidence that this company is not being controlled by a band of brigands, and I submit that point for the consideration of the house.
Now we come to the question of the distribution of this stock. Some hon. members say the stock should be sold only to the public. I confess that that sounds not unreasonable, because during the past years it has come to be a common practice for companies to cut melons, to use very ordinary language which will be understood by everyone. This company does not cut a melon; its stock is sold. The question then arises as to whether or not they are selling it in an unreasonable way. To whom are they selling it? It is being sold to their own stockholders. I have taken the trouble to look up certain information from what was placed before the committee and what appears in the records of the Board of Railway Commissioners, and I find that 95 per cent of the shareholders of this company are in Canada, and over 65 per cent of this stock is owned in this country. Some hon. gentleman said a moment ago that this company is controlled by the American Telephone and Telegraph Company; that is not the case.

That is the case; it has
been so admitted by the Bell Telephone Company.
I will not argue with my hon. friend; I did not ascertain that from the evidence, although I frankly confess that I did not go through it very carefully.
It has been admitted.

I will not dispute that,
but I will say that more than 65 per cent of the stock is owned in Canada. Further, I find that there are about 14,000 shareholders in this company, which is a fairly wide distribution of stock. Even more interesting is the fact that over 10,000 of the shareholders are employees of the company. It is true that they do not hold a very large proportion of the stock, but the aggregate is about

Bell Telephone Company
$4,000,000 or $5,000,000. That is an interesting fact which I think should be taken into consideration by this house.
Who are the people who will be benefited by this issue of stock? It is true that certain large shareholders will benefit; that cannot be disputed, but after when individuals or groups of individuals have given of their best to build up this company and this service and have taken their risks when times were not so good as they are to-day, surely there is nothing sinful or invidious in giving such people a fair chance for a return on their investment. But that is not all; there are over 10,000 employees, and of that number 8,000 are women who, under the distribution of the stock, are subscribers for and owners of stock in the company. These are the people who will benefit by this issue of stock at par.
I merely state these facts in order that we may have before us a picture other than that which has been already drawn. Here is another point. This company can only carry on extensions in two ways, one from the depreciation reserve and the other from new capital. The company must have new capital to make these extensions, and I understand from the evidence produced that the company has in contemplation a very large program of extensions. Surely, in the face of decisions of the railway board and after an examination by a committee of this house, it is not the business of parliament simply because this is a monopoly and a large company to throw obstacles in the way which will prevent the company from carrying on reasonable extensions.
Then there is another point with regard to the railroading of this legislation. I say at once that I do not agree with the method of moving that a bill be reported from the committee of the whole house; frankly I do not agree with it. The only time that power should be exercised is when it has become clearly evident that a certain small groun, whoever they may be, are determined unreasonably to block the fair consideration of legislation.
A statement to that effect was published in the newspapers.

Surely the hon. member
will not suggest that I am trying to block the passage of the bill; I am trying to facilitate it. I simply say that I am not in accord with that method. I was not here the other night; had I been present I would have voted against the proposal, because these
facts should be borne in mind. This bill was introduced on February 15 and had its first reading on that day. That was a long time ago, and the bill was reported to the house from the committee on March 29. It has been on the order paper for weeks and weeks. This is my point: the house and the private bills committee exercise a dual function in regard to private legislation, first, judicial, and second, legislative-or the other way about, whichever way you like to put it. I submit that any private legislation has a right to be considered and to be passed through this, house, and not to be blocked or obstructed.
To be dealt with one way or the other.

To be determined. There is also the question of the consideration of these bills when they return to the house from the private bills committee, or in this case the railway committee. When this bill went before the railway committee, although I was not present I have been informed that it had a normal and fair consideration; there was no attempt to railroad it through that committee, and nobody charges that. There is an old practice of parliament which was most scrupulously observed by the late Sir Wilfrid Lau-rier, by Sir Robert Borden, and by the other leaders of my day, namely, that where private legislation had been referred to a select committee of the house, and was reported by such committee, the house accepted that report as a decision of one of its committees to which had been delegated the consideration of that particular matter. That has been the practice of parliament for many years. It does not mean that all discussion is precluded in regard to the bill, but it does mean that normally parliament is supposed to accept the findings of its own committees appointed for the purpose. It is obvious that other members of the house who are not on these committees cannot hear in the house the evidence and the discussion which the members of the committee heard. The members of the committee are appointed, and it is their duty to determine these matters.
This bill, then, has been before parliament since February 15th. It has been considered by the railway committee. The activities of the company have been considered by the railway board. All of this being before parliament, the bill should receive at least fair consideration. I do not say that hon. members should vote for it-they can vote as they like; that is their privilege. But I do submit that the bill ought to have the opportunity of being determined by the house itself.
Bell Telephone Company

I am not going to detain the house further than to say that as far as I am concerned I have given this matter a great deal of thought. It is my intention to support the bill as reasonable legislation, believing firmly that every precaution has been taken by the measures that I have mentioned to safeguard the public interests.

May I suggest to my hon. friend who has just taken his seat (Mr. Stevens) that for the most part the points he has raised are points that are not before us at all, points about which there is no controversy. My hon. friend asked whether we were to accept the decision of the railway board only when it happened to please us. No one, so far as my hearing goes, has ventured to dispute the railway board's determination as to rate. The dispute was carried through the proper channels to the governor in council, but the decision was not upset. There is no objection in this house to that decision, however much those of us who have to be consumers of the company's products in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec may object to the price that is being charged.
My hon. friend took occasion to dispute the statement that has been made that this was a stock with a guaranteed 8 per cent dividend, and that that devidend was not a high return to the shareholders, particularly when the risks taken by those who first ventured on the enterprise are considered. Mr. Speaker, this question has nothing to do with the matter under discussion. This company was incorporated and entered into business about 1880. It paid 8 per cent the first or second year of its existence, and has been paying 8 per cent every year since. It is not guaranteed in the sense that there is a sealed and delivered guarantee, but the railway board has clearly intimated that it will allow the earnings of the company to be regulated to permit the continuation of that dividend. We passed through a very severe period of depression during the war years, and the company still continued to pay 8 per cent, although it was before the railway board on three different occasions regarding its rates. There is at this moment no question before the house whether the rates are reasonable. I could detain the house for some time on the question of the reasonableness of the rates.
Just a word regarding the distribution of new stock. There is certainly a wide distribution of stock. It was admitted by the Bell Telephone Company, when it was before the railway board, that the American Telephone and Telegraph Company is the body

with control of the Bell company. There are other large shareholders, and I have no doubt a great many employees have been allowed to participate in the purchase of stock, probably on the instalment plan. They are most likely very small shareholders with a share or two apiece, and any dividend which comes to them in the way of an opportunity to subscribe to new stock at par is insignificant. In any case, significant or not, it has nothing to do with the merits of the proposal. It is only put into the discussion in order to draw sympathy for the company's proposition.
Regarding extensions, .the money for this purpose comes from two sources. I agree that it comes from the capital of the company. That capital is raised either by an issue of stock or by an issue of bonds. The company also has what is known as a depreciation withdrawal, amounting I think to about five or six per cent of its total gross income. This percentage is turned back into the company, not to be retained in cash, but for use in connection with depreciation, and repairs. The practice of this company is not to put that money aside, but to put it back into its plant. I have forgotten how many millions of dollars this five or six per cent of the gross income of the company amounts to, but it is used for financing extensions.
The company has been spending at a very great rate during the last few years on the installation of what is called the automatic system of telephones. It has been necessary to scrap many buildings and much equipment, and the depreciation piled up has probably not been equal to the amount of capital destroyed.
I do not expect, Mr. Speaker, the attention of the members on the other side, but I would appreciate not having all this distraction in the chamber, because it makes it quite difficult to talk.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Is the hon. member
referring to me?

I just want to carry on, if
I may. The conversation is a little disturbing.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I did not think I was
disturbing the hon. gentleman.

It is quite all right; I knew my hon. friend did not.
The expenditure of capital has been very serious during the last few years, but the company has maintained this expenditure by dint of certain stock issues, by dint of money got from depreciation, and by dint of certain issues of bonds on the market. The com-

Bell Telephone Company
pany has, as my hon. friend just stated, some $13,000,000 in unissued stock in its treasury, which will be taken up very readily. But more than that they can issue the same value of bonds as there is stock outstanding. If they issued this $13,000,000 of stock it would make $75,000,000 worth of stock. There are bonds outstanding to the amount of $40,000,000; therefore on a fifty-fifty basis they may issue $35,000,000 of bonds-that is, assuming their capitalization is made up of 50 per cent bonds and 50 per cent stock. This is much more than enough, with the depreciation money that comes in every year, to carry on their estimated extensions for, I should say, five years, three or four years even on the company's own statement. Therefore there is no immediate necessity for any authority to issue new stock. Under all the circumstances it is an extravagant thing for the company to ask that its capital stock be increased from $75,000,000 to $150,000,000. It is an extravagant claim, and I think the house might fairly examine it with caution before allowing it.
The company is in a peculiar position in that it is one of a ring of four companies. The parent company of course is that gigantic holding interest known as the American Telephone and Telegraph Company. It controls the Bell Telephone Company, holding some 32 or 33 per cent of its stock. It owns outright the Western Electric Company of Chicago. The Bell Telephone Company and the Western Electric Company in turn have acquired and own all the capital stock of the Northern Electric Company, of which the house has heard. The Western Electric Company make all the apparatus for the American Telephone and Telegraph Company, and the Northern Electric Company make all the apparatus for the Bell Telephone Company. It is idle to say that there is any competition. There is no competition. The Minister of Railways very properly cited a case where certain telephone equipment was bought in the English market.
Very much of it too.

In the city of Winnipeg one or two exchanges are supplied by the Northern Electric Company and one or two by the English concern, but my recollection, subject to correction-and I think I am quite accurate-is that by an arrangement made by the different manufacturers, the English manufacturer cannot come into the market in Ontario and Quebec.
That I do not know. I do not know how you are going to prevent it.

They have done it by arrangement. There were some lawsuits over patents that were settled in that way. Let us, however, leave that aside. The Bell telephone apparatus is absolutely standardized. The English company cannot make it; it is not allowed to make it, because the Northern Electric Company and the Western Electric Company own the use of the patents on the Bell telephone apparatus and nobody can make it outside of them. Therefore the Bell Telephone Company, whether it wishes to do so or not, is restricted to purchasing from its own creature, the Northern Electric Company, all its apparatus.
I am not going to enter into a discussion of prices; that will come when another bill is under discussion. But I say that no satisfactory proof has been given of the correctness of the prices charged by the Northern Electric Company to the Bell Telephone Company. The most that I can find in the judgment of the Board of Railway Commissioners is that the prices are not unreasonable. I do not know how they found that out, because the railway board, under a certain clause in the act which, they said, forbade them to go into the affairs of the Northern Electric, refused to inquire into the affairs of that company, and no one knows what is the proper price of the articles which are supplied by the Northern Electric Company to the Bell Telephone Company. This is rather lengthy and involved. All I want to say and really the only reason I have for referring to that phase of the situation at the moment is this. There is under public bills and orders a bill to which the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) has referred. That bill provides the one thing that the Board of Railway Commissioners found wanting, namely, the power for them to investigate this subsidiary company, the Northern Electric Company, in order to find out whether for the $12,000,000 of money being spent by the Bell Telephone Company over the counter of the Northern Electric Company, the former is getting full value, and whether, if it is not getting full value, it has the value tucked away in the Northern Electric Company, which value should be taken into account by the Board of Railway Commissioners as an asset or as a potential income, which in turn should relieve the consumers of the heavy charges which they are called upon to pay.
Under all these circumstances, and in view of the fact that municipality after municipality, I understand, in Quebec and, I know, in Ontario, have protested and have fought and are not satisfied in regard to the matter,
Bell Telephone Company

I submit to the house and particularly to members from other provinces than Ontario and Quebec that it is only fair that we should first deal with this matter by getting the powers of the railway board so extended that it can investigate the affairs, not of a hotel or a steamship company but of a company that subsists only by reason of its connection with and ownership by the Bell Telephone Company, a company that was started by the Bell Telephone Company, that was brought along by the Bell Telephone Company, that had its business given to it by the Bell Telephone Company, that prospered because of its relationship to the Bell Telephone Company, and that is, in conjunction with the Western Electric Company, owned by the Bell Telephone Company.
If the bill which stands in the name of the hon. gentleman is adopted by the house, will it apply in case the capital of the company .is increased?

Certainly, if we get it
passed. I think it is quite likely that the Board of Railway Commissioners will find, after the investigation which may be authorized by that bill, that there is no need of such capital expenditure as we are now considering and that they will not be called upon to authorize any increase. That really is the ground upon which I think the matter should be considered at the moment. No possible harm can be done by leaving it over if necessary for a year and certainly no harm can be done by leaving it over for a few weeks.
Perhaps at the risk of repetition-of which I am not fond myself and to which I know my hon. friends are not anxious to listen- I might go over once more this feature of the issue of stock that is going to be such a real deterrent to the affairs of the company. The overhead for fixed charges 'and dividends at present is $7,000,000, and for every $100 you allow to be issued by the company in stock, $8 comes from the consumer. For every $100 that the company gets on a bond, from $4.50 to $5 is borne by the consumer. Is it not therefore essential that those who are consumers and those of us who represent them should consider the matter very carefully? On only two occasions that I know of has the company _ failed to have any issue of stock taken up by its shareholders, and on those two occasions the company went into the market. On the first occasion the stock was down around par and they got in the market an average of $102.50; that is, for every $100, $2.50 more went into the com-

pany's coffers to build up its plant than would have gone had the shareholders taken up the stock. On the other occasion they sold the stock at $125, so that on that occasion $25 more was realized to the coffers of the company than would have been realized had the shareholders taken up the stock. While the stock may be borne down, while the market price may suffer if a large block is thrown on the market, it suffers inappreciably if we consider a recent issue of stock where the rights that accrued to shareholders-that is, the right to subscribe for one new share at $100 for every four shares held-have' been sold on the market at a premium. Those rights to-day would easily bring $10 per right. That is an extra dividend to the shareholder of 10 per cent which comes out of the consumer in the year in which the stock issue is made. That has been the practice with many companies, but this is a public utility company which has received great advantages from the parliament of Canada. It is allowed to go here and there at its own will and pleasure, planting its poles and stringing its wires without paying one cent for its right of way. Therefore, not only because of its peculiar situation in that regard, but because of the intimate nature of its dealings with the people and the necessity of the people patronizing it-, we are entitled to handle, not too roughly, not too tenderly, that creature of our own so that it may do business in a fair way, and I think the consumer who is obliged to consume its products should be treated as fairly as the company is treated. That, I think, is all anyone can ask, and I would submit that at this moment the fair way to treat this bill is to postpone this discussion.
I do not want to talk any longer. I do not want to run the risk of anyone suggesting that I am talking this bill out. I am doing nothing of the sort; I do not agree with that method; but I think this bill might well stand until the other bill comes up and is disposed of. No harm can possibly come by postponing this discussion, because the company has all the capital it will require, by any stretch of the imagination, for the next few years, and when the time approaches when more money is required and the issue of capital stock is an absolute necessity, then may be the time when we can deal fairly with the matter. I venture this statement, not as an authority on finance, but by every rule that I have heard, that it is good business to arrange your capital on the basis of 50 per cent bonds and 50 per cent capital stock. If 50 per cent is bonds and 50 per cent capital stock, you are doing the fair thing. The

Bell Telephone Company
people presented to the railway board the proposition, that- bonds should be 60 per cent and stock 40 per cent, but leaving it at bonds 50 per cent and capital stock 50 per cent-and the company has not come to that point, for many years at least-the company can then with very great advantage to the consumers raise all the money that is required at 5 per cent, instead of coming here and getting permission to go out and give bonuses to its shareholders and pay 8 per cent on every $100 they raise by issue of capital stock.

This bill, innocent as it looks, is very far-reaching in its possible effects. It simply asks permission to allow the Bell Telephone Company to increase its capital stock from $75,000,000 to $150,000,000; in other words, to double its stock. I think it is the duty of parliament at this time to inquire carefully into every feature connected with this application before it is granted. This is, in fact, an application by a great American company which, like a vast great octopus, is reaching out to secure a monopoly of the telephone and telegraph business over the whole North American continent. Not only does it seek to control the rates of service to the people, but it has also a monopoly of all the supplies which are used by the parent company. This is being accomplished by the great American Telephone and Telegraph Company of New York, which is practically the chief owner of the Bell Telephone Company. Subsidiaries have been established for this purpose, and it is highly important, I think, that the people should know the full import and purpose of this application.
There is a bill before the House of Commons to compel an investigation into all subsidiary companies controlled or owned by the telephone or telegraph companies, subsidiaries such as the Northern Electric, which are manufacturing for and supplying the parent company. When a private company owns a public utility, it is surely right that the people should have all the data concerning the working of that company, and know whether it owns certain subsidiaries in which it can hide its vast profits, and thus furnish it with an excuse to ask for an increase of rates to bleed the public. It is certainly not in the interests of the people that the stock of any company should be indiscriminately increased. This allows the company concerned to hide its real profits.
In an article that appeared recently in the Toronto Globe, written by one Mr. R.
A. Reid, who very vigorously opposed the application of the Bell Telephone Company before the board of railway commissioners for an increase in its rates, and who is also opposing its application for an increase in capital, there is the complaint that with the sanction of the Dominion government and by order of the Board of Railway Commissioners the telephone rates of the Bell Telephone Company were increased to the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, putting an additional burden of $2,600,000 a year, through this public utility, on the people who use it. This was done ostensibly through the Bell Telephone Company, but really for the sake of the great American Telephone and Telegraph Company of New York. I think it is time that the people of Canada knew that the Bell Telephone Company is simply a name under which the American Telephone and Telegraph Company of New York is reaching out to exploit the people all over the North American continent. It adopts this method in order to avoid any feeling of prejudice against the parent concern as a foreign company.
This bill, in my opinion, seeks to make the greatest amount of plucking with the least squawking possible. In the matter of the application to raise its rates last year, there was no legal or logical reason, according to Mr. Reid, who has been writing in the Toronto Globe, for granting the increase. It was granted without any specific or definite evidence being presented by the company in the most important issues raised at the hearing before the Board of Railway Commissioners. To me it looked like a typical case where a company holds a charter to own and operate a public utility for the sake of gain. The wonder to me is that the people after all these years will still put up with it. Surely the evil of having a public utility such as the telephone in the hands of private companies is well illustrated in the application contained in this bill.
Another thing which we may well marvel at is that men in this house who at the last election pledged themselves on public platforms before their electors to look after the interests of the people particularly, now seem willing to barter the people's rights to powerful combines and interests in control of these public utilities. The first commercial telephone used in Canada was established in 1877 in the city of Hamilton, and it is rather strange that after all this time, fifty-one years,
Bell Telephone Company

the ownership and control of a public utility of this kind should be in private hands. One would have thought that public opinion would have expressed itself so strongly before this that it would have been impossible for a bill of this kind to come before parliament. Of course, parliament since that time seems to have existed very largely to find means of fleecing the people in the interests of some private concern or other.
In the west we have for a long time been dealing with this question of public ownership. Really public ownership has been forced on us in the three prairie provinces simply by the failure of private ownership. Looking back over the years since I came to Canada, it does seem to me that not one public utility in private hands has ever been a success; either the people have been fleeced to meet undue profits, or else through incompetency there has been failure. This has been true in western Canada ever since the Canadian Pacific Railway gave to grain companies who would construct elevators on their sidings a monopoly of their oars to handle the farmers' grain. Through that procedure we have suffered all kinds of abuses, and farming in all the western country has been made a most precarious calling down through the years. The people had no way of redress; in weights, grades, dockage and prices they were simply robbed of their earnings. Indeed1 we can look at other great public utilities too, suoh as the railways, private ownership of which has landed us in the financial perplexity which we as a nation are not clear of yet. When we talk to-day of the tremendous cost to the country of the Canadian National Railways as a public utility, it should be borne in mind that it was due to their failure under private ownership.
Now, seeing that the telephone business is a public utility, since it can be so readily established by the people themselves, it is a wonder that a bill of this kind is before parliament. I know it will be said that a great sacrifice was made for the sake of western Canada in respect of many public utilities which we now enjoy, particularly the railways; but the west never landed this country in the tremendous amount of debt which we have had to meet on these great public utilities as did eastern Canada. As an example, take the old Grand Trunk Railway Company, which has cost Canada untold loss, which was not all a direct financial loss either, great as that was, but indirectly a loss of national prestige, something that we are now endeavouring to buy back.

But the Canadian National Railway redemption is not all that our railway service has cost the Dominion. If everything be reckoned, the Canadian Pacific Railway has cost the people perhaps more than the Canadian National Railway ever did. This was due to the tremendous mistake away back in the eighties of letting that great public utility fall into private hands. We must count the cost of some twenty-six million acres of the best of our land, to say nothing of railway lines completed and handed over, to which must be added twenty years' taxes bn that land, and the tremendous inconvenience to settlers in establishing those essentials of civilization, good roads and schools, on which they had to pay the taxes themselves.
Now, it seems strange that men can be found who will favour these exploiting concerns and grant charters to companies who own public utilities for private gain. When we count the cash paid out for the redemption of what is now the Canadian National Railway system, it is a very little thing indeed compared with the cost of these things. I apologize for even mentioning the railway question, but I do so to show the debacle we are landing ourselves in through private ownership of other public utilities. In Saskatchewan we have had government ownership of our telephones practically from the start, and I would advise the people of Ontario and Quebec to lose no time in securing control of this great public utility, which has become a necessity in our complicated civilization as compared with the days of not very long ago. In that western province, with its much more scattered population than eastern Canada and no big cities, we have a telephone service at a cost that is surprisingly low when it is remembered that we have to go much further to find a subscriber than would be the case in rural Ontario. The installation of a rural telephone line is spread over a number of years, and the debentures are redeemed by a tax rate which is hardly felt. At the present time we pay about $28 for a city telephone. I find that in the city of Ottawa the people are paying $39.60 for a desk phone. Our telephone lines cover practically the whole province. Only in the newer settlements are the people without this utility.
I do not think anyone in western Canada today would think of going back to private ownership in relation to the telephone service.
If parliament passes this bill it will be another means of robbing the worker of his earnings and concentrating the country's wealth and giving a power obtained by money

Bell Telephone Company
control, and it will make a still further dividing line between the worker and the government. From the Globe of March 29 last I clipped the following from a letter written by R. A. Reid:
It was shown and conclusively proved at the recent Bell Telephone rate case hearings that this concern has continuously over a period of years issued its stock at par value of $100 to its shareholders, when that same stock was selling on the market at prices ranging from $125 up to $150 per share.
Will anyone say in the face of this that this bill should be passed'? It is rather strange to me, since this statement has been published in a paper like the Toronto Globe, that the people are not even now organizing to promote public or government ownership. If what I have read is true-and I have never seen it refuted-it means that when this stock is selling on the market at $150 per share and is issued to the shareholders at $100, as it usually is, every issue of $10,000,000 worth of stock represents a bonus or a present of $5,000,000 to the shareholders. The result is that every user of telephones on their lines, be he rich or poor, must continue in his sweated labour to pay for it. This is a practice which should not under any circumstances be allowed. The telephone business here, connected as it is with the American Telegraph and Telephone Company of New York, is virtually a monopoly, and to me it is rather a sad fact that a Liberal government of Canada should further a monopoly which has in view the fleecing of the entire public. The company has been able to do as it pleases so far as rates are concerned. In the United States it does over 72 per cent of the telephone business and dominates all the others. The same journal says, further, that it has worked the " holding company " device to an extent unrivalled in any other industry. This holding company device is a legal scheme for confusing the public and investigators and for getting something for nothing.
I trust that even yet the people of this country, and this parliament will see better than to support a proposal of this nature and to pass a bill like this, which is nothing more than an attempt to give power to a great monopoly to fleece the public of its earnings.

The amendment proposed by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) asks that this bill be not read the third time but be referred back to the committee of the whole to be amended by adding section 3 to provide that no issue of capital stock of the Bell Telephone Company Limited shall be made
except it is offered to the public for subscription. I may say in connection with this amendment that the whole subject was before the Board of Railway Commissioners and considerable objection was taken to the methods pursued by this particular company. The stock has been quoted at 170 and the company has made handouts to a few favourites within the charmed circle-so much so that in the opinion of many the company is not altogether complying with the law. Let me point out in the first place that the American Telephone and Telegraph Company owns 98 per cent of the stock of the Western Electric. This will give you an idea of the way these various companies are interlocked. In the second place the Western Electric Company owns 48 per cent of the Northern Electric. The third point I wish the house to grasp is that the Bell Telephone Company owns 52 per cent of the Northern Electric. And in the fourth place the American Telephone and Telegraph Company controls them all. In other words, all these these concerns constitute a combine in restraint of trade. That is all they are. They are interlocked and are a part of this gigantic trust-the American trust to which I have referred. We seem to be very fortunate in this country in our trusts; we make it possible for them to flourish in Canada, so that they may exploit the people in connection with telephones, telephone apparatus, pulpwood, power and so on. Canada is the happy hunting ground for speculators from the other side. They come here and by means of agreements drawn up by clever lawyers they get around our financial statutes. The result is that many of these companies are an affliction worse than the family compact.
Let me give a little bit of the history of this corporation to show the way they have been jockeying with the law. Its record justifies the very wide amendment proposed by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland). We had a parallel case in the history of the gas company of Toronto, in connection with which an appeal was made to the legislature to prevent the adoption of just such a principle as is laid down in this bill. It would be interesting to know what regulations the Board of Railway Commissioners have over the issue of stock by this company. I fail to see any regulations regarding the sale of this $75,000,000, or any regulations providing for subscription to this stock. Dear knows to what extent the American Telephone and Telegraph Company are interested in this $75,000,000. In view of all that, and in view of the existence of this trust which flourishes in Canada like a green bay tree, I think we

Bell Telephone Company

should know something of the. history of the various issues of stock of this company. The company was incorporated in 1880. They came back to parliament in 1882 asking for authority to issue more stock, and in 1884 they came back again. They seem to have come back every five or six years, after changes of government, looking for amendments to their charter and for authority to issue additional stock. However, I have yet to find that the stock was sold by public subscription, as is proposed in the amendment before the house. In 1892 they again came to parliament and received authority to issue more stock; in 1894 they renewed their application, and returned again after a change of government in 1896. In 1902 they had a new act passed conferring various powers on them. Four years later they returned again and were given power to increase their stock issue, but nothing was said as to how the stock should be issued. Then in 1920 they had another act passed by this parliament giving them power to deal with their stock again. Now they are back again asking leave to increase their capitalization from $75,000,000 to $150,000,000, but they give no intimation of what they propose to do with the stock or why it is necessary to issue these, additional shares, although they say they wish to undertake extensions. Is this new stock issue to go to the present shareholders, or is it to be divided up all along the line? When you pay for hydro electric power you simply pay the cost price; in Ontario the rate per kilowatt hour is only It- cents as compared with oi to 4 cents in Buffalo and Montreal. This company is under the control of the railway commission, who have failed in their duty by not making some regulations to cover the disposal of this stock.

I rise to a point of order. The hon. gentleman may say whatever he wishes so long as he observes the rules of the house, but under the rules he cannot criticize the Board of Railway Commissioners as he has been doing.

The Board of Railway
Commissioners is a court of record, and therefore may not be attacked except by way of impeachment. This has been decided twice by this house within my knowledge.

In order to show that
public subscription should be allowed I think it only fair that I should refer to the history of past issues of stock by this company, to show how the stock was sold then. I notice some hon. gentlemen are smiling; this is not going to be a laughing matter to the poor people of Ontario and Quebec who will have to pay an additional charge for the use of their telephones. Some of these gentlemen who

are now smiling would do better to stand up and support this amendment in order to prevent the stock being parcelled out among the favourites and insiders of the company.
Now I would like to refer to the way in which previous stock issues have been disposed of. On December 31, 1925, the authorized capital of this company amounted to $75,000,000; of that amount $50,000,000 had been issued. In December, 1899, stock was sold privately to a few favourites at $100 per share while the market price was $193, and the very same thing will be done with this next issue of stock if this amendment is not adopted. In 1900 the company sold $50,000 worth of stock at a net premium of $35,105, and in May of 1902, $1,000,000 in stock was sold to the inside people for $125 per share, although the market price was $176. From these figures the house will see how the people of this country have been held up. Where do the consumers and the general public come in when this sort of thing goes on?

I have spoken to the' leaders of the different parties and to different members of the house and I gather that this would suit the Convenience of members better than sitting late Saturday evening. If the1 house will give its consent I should like to move:
That on Saturday the 19th instant the house shall meet at two o'clock in the afternoon.
That is with the understanding that we will adjourn at six o'clock, and applies to this coming Saturday only.
